summary: Defines MIB objects for managing the Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism of Protocol Independent Multicast. Network management tools can use them. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: This is a control panel layout, in a form network tools understand, for monitoring how multicast routers choose their helper.

what tables are in the pim bsr mib
subtitle: The SNMP management objects for watching and configuring the Bootstrap Router mechanism of PIM multicast routers.

tldr.problem: PIM routers use a Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism to learn which router acts as the Rendezvous Point for each multicast group range, but operators had no standard way to inspect or configure that mechanism over SNMP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5240 defines the PIM-BSR-MIB module with four tables (Candidate-RP, Elected BSR RP-Set, Candidate-BSR and Elected-BSR) plus two notifications about BSR elections.
tldr.outcome: Management tools get a common view of who is a candidate, who won the election and which group-to-RP mappings are in use. The RFC also warns that write access to these objects can disrupt multicast service.

today: RFC 5240 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It assigns the object identifier { mib-2 172 } to the module.

sections.title: Introduction and Origin
sections.content:
RFC 5240 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing the Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism of Protocol Independent Multicast (PIM). The BSR mechanism itself is described in RFC 4601 and RFC 5059.

The document was created by moving some of the PIM BSR-specific tables out of an earlier version of the PIM MIB, which was published as RFC 5060. The MIB module is written in SMIv2 and is accessed through SNMP, as laid out in the Internet-Standard Management Framework (RFC 3410).
sections.eli5: Think of a big instruction manual that got too thick. The authors took the chapter about one special job and made it a booklet of its own.

sections.title: Four Tables Describe the BSR Mechanism
sections.content:
The module has four tables. Which tables are populated depends on the role the router plays.

  • The Candidate-RP Table has one row for each multicast group prefix for which the local router is configured to advertise itself as a Candidate-RP (C-RP). It exists on routers configured as Candidate-RP.
  • The Elected BSR RP-Set Table has one row for each group-to-RP mapping received in C-RP advertisements. It exists on an elected BSR (E-BSR).
  • The Candidate-BSR Table has one row for each Candidate-BSR configuration of the local router. It exists on routers configured as Candidate-BSR.
  • The Elected-BSR Table has one row for each elected BSR. It exists on a router that is an elected BSR.

Address-valued objects use the textual conventions from the INET-ADDRESS-MIB (RFC 4001).
sections.eli5: There are four lists. One says who volunteered to be a helper, one lists the helpers the boss has heard about, one says who volunteered to be the boss, and one says who won.

sections.title: What Each Table Holds
sections.content:
The Candidate-RP Table is indexed by the Candidate-RP address and the group prefix (group address plus prefix length). Its readable and writable columns include whether the range is advertised as a BIDIR-PIM or PIM-SM group range, the time left before the next Candidate-RP-Advertisement, the priority, the advertisement interval and the holdtime.

The Elected BSR RP-Set Table is indexed by the group prefix and the RP address. All its data columns are read-only: the priority, the holdtime, the time before the entry ages out and whether the range is BIDIR-PIM. The RFC says an elected BSR uses this table to create Bootstrap messages after applying a local policy to include some or all of the mappings.

The Candidate-BSR Table and the Elected-BSR Table are both indexed by a zone index. The Candidate-BSR row holds the address, priority, hash mask length, whether this router is the elected BSR and the time before the next Bootstrap message. The Elected-BSR row reports the elected BSR's address, priority, hash mask length and the time before it will be declared down.

Rows in the configurable tables use a RowStatus column for creating and deleting entries and a StorageType column that defaults to nonVolatile.
sections.eli5: Each list is like a class roster. Some rosters you can edit, like signing up to volunteer. Others you can only read, like the final results board.

sections.title: Defaults, Ranges and Priorities
sections.content:
Several objects carry defaults and limits that the module spells out.

  • Candidate-RP priority: range 0 to 255, default 192.
  • Candidate-RP advertisement interval: 1 to 26214 seconds, default 60.
  • Candidate-RP holdtime: 0 to 65535 seconds, default 150. The value can be zero only when the C-RP is shutting down.
  • Candidate-BSR priority: range 0 to 255, default 0.
  • Candidate-BSR hash mask length: 0 to 128. It defaults to 30 for IPv4 and 126 for IPv6.

Priorities run in opposite directions for the two roles. For an RP in the Elected BSR RP-Set Table, numerically higher values mean lower priority and zero is the highest priority. For BSRs, numerically higher values mean higher priority.
sections.eli5: Each setting has a starting value and a limit, like a volume dial that starts at a set spot and cannot go past the ends. Watch out: for helpers a smaller number wins, but for bosses a bigger number wins.

sections.title: Election Notifications
sections.content:
The module defines two notifications, both tied to the election of a BSR for PIM.

  • pimBsrElectedBSRLostElection should be generated when the current E-BSR loses an election to a new Candidate-BSR. It carries the address type, address and priority of the elected BSR. It is generated when pimBsrCandidateBSRElectedBSR becomes FALSE.
  • pimBsrCandidateBSRWinElection should be generated when a C-BSR wins the BSR election. It is generated when pimBsrCandidateBSRElectedBSR becomes TRUE.

For both, the RFC states that only an E-BSR should generate the notification.
sections.eli5: When the boss changes, the system can ring a bell once so the people watching know there is a new boss.

sections.title: Compliance and Groups
sections.content:
The compliance statement applies to PIM routers that implement the BSR mechanism. The mandatory group, pimBsrObjectGroup, lists the objects from all four tables. The notification group, pimBsrDiagnosticsGroup, is optional.

The module sits under pimBsrMIB, with notifications, objects and conformance as its three branches.
sections.eli5: To say a router follows the rules it must support the main list of items. The bell notifications are an optional extra.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Objects with read-write or read-create access can be sensitive. The RFC gives two examples: a new Candidate-BSR with a high priority, or a raised priority on an existing one, can take over the elected BSR role and disrupt services. A new Candidate-RP with a lower priority number, or a changed priority, can force other routers to select it for a group prefix and disrupt services through that prefix.

Even reading is sensitive: GET operations can reveal the elected BSR, the Candidate-BSRs and the Candidate-RPs, which could help prepare a denial-of-service attack. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, so the RFC RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features and says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: If a stranger can edit the volunteer list, they could sneak in as boss and cause trouble. Even peeking at the list helps them plan. So keep the list locked.
